item.text: {"chapter_id":"4B","judge_orientation":"Retain a balanced, passage-supported record: 2023 evidence shows executive efforts that threatened electoral, transparency, media, surveillance, and civilian institutional safeguards, alongside functioning opposition mobilization, judicial review, electoral administration, formal rights, some inclusion reforms, and international cooperation. Attribution remains uneven for national abuses and agency-level failures. The future judge should distinguish inherited or pre-2023 conditions from 2023 conduct and should not treat judicial or civic constraints as voluntary restraint by López Obrador.","entries":[{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0051-E019","reason_to_read":"Compact mixed synthesis of the 2023 electoral and institutional conflict, including Plan B, pressure on autonomous bodies, judicial intervention, and continuing electoral administration.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["4B.1","4B.2","4B.4","4B.10"],"corrected_summary":"CSIS described budget cuts and political pressure affecting autonomous institutions and a Plan B that reduced the electoral authority’s powers. It also reported that courts suspended or invalidated important provisions and that the INE conducted successful and transparent local elections in June 2023; these constraints demonstrate institutional resilience, not necessarily voluntary executive restraint."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0012-E013","reason_to_read":"Direct 2023 evidence of the proposed electoral changes and their ruler attribution.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.1","4B.2","4B.4"],"corrected_summary":"López Obrador backed Plan B, which the Senate approved in February 2023 and which would reduce the electoral institute’s size, budget, supervisory and sanctioning powers, and local-office staffing. At the time of the report, enactment remained pending and the final judicial outcome was not yet reported."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0048-E006","reason_to_read":"Detailed institutional assessment of the proposed electoral reform’s effects on election administration, fiscal oversight, professional staffing, and inclusion.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.1","4B.2","4B.4","4B.7"],"corrected_summary":"The INE warned that Plan B would weaken its autonomy, territorial and professional capacity, electoral training, fiscal oversight, data protection, local bodies, and affirmative-action and gender-equality structures. These were institutional warnings about anticipated consequences, not proof that every consequence occurred."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0043-E010","reason_to_read":"Direct evidence that independent electoral and judicial institutions halted implementation during 2023.","role":"favorable","supported_lenses":["4B.1","4B.4","4B.10"],"corrected_summary":"After the Supreme Court provisionally suspended Plan B, the INE unanimously paused implementation in March 2023 and resumed operating under the prior rules pending final review, preserving organizational continuity and stated electoral and privacy safeguards. The passage does not show López Obrador’s personal compliance or approval."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0055-E006","reason_to_read":"Primary legal record of the National Guard transfer and the scope and timing of judicial correction.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.2","4B.4","4B.5","4B.9"],"corrected_summary":"The Supreme Court invalidated key portions of the executive-originated scheme transferring National Guard operational and administrative control, command-related powers, and specified transitional provisions to the Defense Ministry. The invalidity effects were postponed until January 1, 2024, so the ruling did not immediately reverse the arrangement during 2023."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0047-E013","reason_to_read":"Strong, specific evidence of executive and coalition obstruction of the independent transparency agency, plus judicial checking.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.3","4B.4","4B.6","4B.9"],"corrected_summary":"HRW reported that López Obrador vetoed two Senate-approved INAI appointments, legislators from his party rejected another proposal, and the agency consequently lacked the quorum needed to meet or decide cases; the report also described repeated proposals to eliminate INAI and a substantially repeated transparency-secrecy order after the Supreme Court struck down the first."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0026-E020","reason_to_read":"Adds the 2023 quorum, backlog, proposed biometric database, and later judicial repair while separating pre-existing surveillance law from new proposals.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["4B.4","4B.9","4B.10"],"corrected_summary":"During 2023 INAI lacked its required quorum and had nearly 6,000 pending cases; López Obrador and allies supported dissolving it, while the Supreme Court later allowed four commissioners to meet. Existing metadata-access rules included judicial safeguards for historical data, and a proposed biometric identity system raised privacy concerns without being shown as implemented."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0029-E006","reason_to_read":"Direct ruler-attributed evidence of public attacks on investigative journalists and a press-freedom organization during 2023.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.3","4B.6"],"corrected_summary":"In 2023 López Obrador repeatedly criticized Article 19, Proceso, Animal Político, Aristegui Noticias, and reporter Nayeli Roldán over spyware reporting, calling Roldán unobjective and unprofessional and accusing Article 19 of foreign funding. The affected journalists and organizations reported increased abuse, threats, stalking, and safety concerns; the passage does not establish that he ordered those subsequent threats."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0012-E008","reason_to_read":"Target-period evidence separating state-attributed press aggression from private or criminal violence and linking some attacks to presidential rhetoric.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.3","4B.6"],"corrected_summary":"ARTICLE 19 recorded 561 press aggressions in 2023, including 106 classified as illegitimate public-power use; the Mexican state was identified as the largest category of aggressor, with 91 federal-level cases. The report also identified at least ten private attacks using language repeated from presidential conferences, while not attributing every attack to López Obrador."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0014-E004","reason_to_read":"Distinct 2023 evidence on public advertising concentration as a media-independence mechanism.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.6"],"corrected_summary":"Freedom House reported that the López Obrador administration failed to deliver an effective state-advertising framework; ten media and communication companies received 45.05 percent of official advertising in 2023, and 2.559 billion of 2.978 billion pesos appropriated was spent. The figures do not prove political favoritism or altered content."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0014-E006","reason_to_read":"Most direct reopened evidence on surveillance, procurement disclosure, and lack of accountability during the target period.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.3","4B.9"],"corrected_summary":"Investigations linked military or government agencies to Pegasus and other spyware targeting journalists, human-rights defenders, and investigators; López Obrador denied or minimized the allegations. INAI ordered SEDENA in January 2023 to search for and disclose Pegasus contracts, but SEDENA did not comply for more than a year. Some targeting findings remained investigative rather than final judicial determinations."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0045-E001","reason_to_read":"Direct evidence on proposed regression in political representation for historically discriminated groups.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.1","4B.2","4B.7"],"corrected_summary":"INE participants warned that Plan B would limit the INE’s affirmative-action authority and reduce represented spaces for historically discriminated groups from 65 to 25, without contextual analysis or clear allocation criteria. The passage records institutional criticism of a proposal, not uniform implementation or a final court determination."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0003-E013","reason_to_read":"Balanced target-period evidence of nationwide formal inclusion reforms and continuing implementation barriers.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["4B.7"],"corrected_summary":"In 2023 same-sex marriage was available in all 32 states, 21 states allowed simplified gender-marker changes, Congress approved disability-rights reforms, and Mexico ratified the Inter-American Convention on Older Persons. The same passage reports continuing barriers for people with disabilities and does not establish López Obrador’s personal authorship or uniform implementation."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0031-E004","reason_to_read":"Direct evidence on succession management and attempts to shape post-term political power.","role":"adverse","supported_lenses":["4B.2","4B.5","4B.8"],"corrected_summary":"In June 2023, López Obrador was reported to have announced future reforms affecting judicial selection and National Guard control, supported allocating legislative and cabinet roles to Morena primary runners-up, and used morning conferences to shape the succession and promote his preferred political narrative. The passage describes proposals and strategy, not enacted reforms or a constitutional breach of the presidential term."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0026-E016","reason_to_read":"Evidence on progovernment online networks, attacks on a Supreme Court president, and public-resource-linked information activity, with attribution limits preserved.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["4B.3","4B.6","4B.9"],"corrected_summary":"Freedom House reported a March 2023 campaign of more than 20,000 messages targeting Supreme Court president Norma Piña, a progovernment video network using unsubstantiated claims, and public-resource-supported InfodemiaMX and presidential fact-checking segments criticized as biased or misleading. It also noted no proof that at least one supportive network was financed by the government or party."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0003-E016","reason_to_read":"Specific mixed evidence on an initial accountability initiative followed by failure to compel military disclosure in the Ayotzinapa investigation.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["4B.4","4B.5","4B.9","4B.10"],"corrected_summary":"López Obrador created a truth commission, appointed a special prosecutor, invited independent experts, and ordered government cooperation on Ayotzinapa, but HRW reported that he did not use his authority to compel the military to release key evidence and defended the military while the investigation stalled. The source’s characterization of willingness is evaluative and does not establish personal intent by judicial finding."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0013-E003","reason_to_read":"Expert investigative evidence preserving both obstruction and investigative progress.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["4B.4","4B.9","4B.10"],"corrected_summary":"The GIEI reported continuing obstruction, falsification or concealment of information, withdrawn arrest warrants, pressure on the special prosecutor, and delays, while also recognizing significant advances by Fiscal Omar Gómez and his team. The report attributes conduct to multiple agencies and does not prove López Obrador personally directed each obstruction or correction."},{"evidence_id":"BATCH-0049-E011","reason_to_read":"Independent contrary evidence of government openness and cooperation with external scrutiny, alongside unresolved rights failures.","role":"mixed","supported_lenses":["4B.3","4B.4","4B.7","4B.10"],"corrected_summary":"At the government’s invitation, the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention received full and unimpeded access in September 2023 and acknowledged reforms, releases, and cooperation. It nevertheless found arbitrary detention widespread, including concerns about militarized policing, pressure on judges, discrimination, and weak accountability. The findings are preliminary and do not assign López Obrador personal responsibility for every violation."}],"changes_from_draft":["Added direct 2023 Plan B, INE, INAI, succession, advertising, surveillance, inclusion, press-rhetoric, and Ayotzinapa evidence.","Added favorable or constraining evidence on INE operation, judicial review, formal inclusion reforms, and UN access and cooperation.","Narrowed attribution for aggregate press violence, agency-level failures, surveillance allegations, inclusion reforms, and Ayotzinapa obstruction.","Removed reliance on BATCH-0003-E004 as 2023 evidence because its judicial-reform event is from 2024; retained no unsupported 2024 reform claim.","Corrected the National Guard summary to state that the transfer operated during 2023 but judicial invalidity took effect in 2024.","Separated formal rights, institutional operation, anticipated reform effects, and de facto implementation rather than compressing them into one claim."],"unresolved_gaps":["Direct 2023 evidence of a verified opposition electoral victory, alternation outcome, or López Obrador accepting an electoral loss remains limited; the 2022 recall and Aguascalientes records are contextual rather than 2023 ruler-period evidence.","The reopened passages do not provide a complete personnel audit, civil-service record, or systematic evidence on appointments across the administration.","Equal political access evidence is stronger for formal reforms and proposed affirmative-action changes than for implementation across Indigenous, Afro-Mexican, disability, opposition-region, and other groups.","The record does not establish the final 2023 operational compliance with the National Guard judgment or the executive’s personal response after all Plan B rulings.","Surveillance evidence establishes serious allegations, institutional noncompliance, and delayed investigation, but not a complete chain from López Obrador personally to each operation or target.","The UN Working Group evidence is preliminary and concerns broad state conditions; it should not be treated as a direct measure of presidential responsibility for each detention or judicial-pressure incident."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["The future judge should reopen the full ledger for direct 2023 election outcomes, opposition victories, and transfer-related conduct before relying heavily on 4B.1 or 4B.8.","The future judge should compare the full ledger for whether judicial and electoral constraints were followed in practice after the 2023 rulings, including the delayed National Guard correction.","The future judge should inspect the complete evidence on appointments, CNDH, IFT, COFECE, INAI, civil-service neutrality, and party succession to distinguish isolated vacancies from systematic capture.","The future judge should reopen the full surveillance and media ledger to separate lawful or disputed security activity, military agency conduct, presidential rhetoric, public-resource propaganda, and verified remedies.","The future judge should compare inclusion evidence across formal law, representation, consultation, enforcement, and outcomes, avoiding credit for inherited or merely enacted protections.","The future judge should preserve disagreement between favorable institutional resilience and adverse executive pressure rather than treating either side as dispositive." ]}
